name: ltl2ba
desc: Translate LTL formulae to Buchi automata
why: Turns linear temporal logic formulas into Büchi automata, a real formal-methods transform you can run and watch produce automata.

brief.what_it_is: LTL2BA is a translator that takes a linear temporal logic (LTL) formula and produces a Büchi automaton for it. The homepage offers a web form where you type a formula, pick output options (Spin syntax, verbose mode, statistics, simplification passes), and get back a drawn automaton image or a Spin never claim. The page doesn't describe a command-line install in detail, though the project is listed with an ltl2ba executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The page presents it as a fast LTL to Büchi automata translation, based on the paper "Fast LTL to Büchi Automata Translation" presented at CAV '01. Its stated use is producing never claims that can be fed to the Spin model checker to verify properties of a system.
brief.how_it_works: The form accepts propositional symbols, boolean operators (!, ->, <->, &&, ||), and temporal operators (G, F, U, R, X), with no operator priority so parentheses are required. Options include on-the-fly simplification, a posteriori simplification, strongly connected components simplification, and drawing the generalised Büchi automaton or the Büchi automaton via dot from Graphviz. The page does not explain the translation algorithm itself beyond the paper reference.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no install steps beyond the Download LTL2BA link, which has no URL in the page text. The web version has a 1 GB memory limit and a 2 hour time limit. Drawing automata relies on dot from the Graphviz package. A Java interface, JLtl2Ba, is mentioned but not described.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived academic tool that reads Spin's formula syntax and emits Spin never claims, so it plugs directly into a well-known model checker. The homepage also runs it as a web form that draws the automaton for you.
brief.status: Unknown. The page credits Denis Oddoux (v1.0) and Paul Gastin (v1.2 and v1.3) and mentions Spin 4.3.0, but gives no release date or last-commit information, and I did not fetch a download or repository page.
brief.caveats: The web server's security settings make some formulas containing '!' return a 403 error; the page says to use uppercase NOT for negation in those cases. The web form is limited to 1 GB memory and 2 hours. The page gives no licence information. The README-equivalent is only a web form page, so command-line usage and platform details are unverified.
quotes: LTL 2 BA : fast translation from LTL formulae to Büchi automata
Warning: Due to some security settings on the web server (preventing code injections) some formulae containing negations '!' induce an error (403).
Our program can draw automatically the resulting automaton, and can also print a never claim that can be given to the Spin model checker to verify properties on a system.

judge.reason: A runnable LTL-to-Büchi translation makes temporal logic tangible by turning properties into automata and Spin-checkable claims, a worthwhile formal-methods rabbit hole.

entry.title: ltl2ba
entry.tldr: Turns a linear temporal logic formula, such as 'always, if request then eventually grant', into a Büchi automaton you can feed to the Spin model checker.
entry.deeper_look:
ltl2ba takes a formula in linear temporal logic (LTL) and produces a Büchi automaton: a small state machine that accepts exactly the infinite behaviours the formula describes. Its stated use is to print a Spin "never claim", which the Spin model checker can use to verify properties of a system. The homepage also runs it as a web form that draws the automaton for you.

The input uses propositional symbols, boolean operators (!, ->, <->, &&, ||) and temporal operators (G, F, U, R, X). There is no operator priority, so parentheses are required. The options include several simplification passes and a choice between drawing the generalised Büchi automaton or the Büchi automaton, rendered through dot from Graphviz.

The idea underneath is that a statement about time, like "this never happens" or "this keeps happening", can be compiled into a machine that reads a run of a system and checks it. That is the core trick behind a large family of model checkers. The tool is based on the paper "Fast LTL to Büchi Automata Translation" from CAV '01, and it is a small, old, academic program, so it is a good way to watch that translation happen.
entry.install:
brew install ltl2ba
# Drawing automata relies on dot from Graphviz: brew install graphviz

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage text for the command-line translator, so you can see which options your build supports.
